lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Here is the bootstrap as a machine: the fifteen law schools as tokens. <bookmark mark='b'/> Draw a school at random, copy it down, put it back, and draw again, fifteen times. Some schools are copied twice or three times, some not at all. That's a resample: a new dataset of the same size, drawn with replacement from the sample. <bookmark mark='c'/> Compute its correlation, and drop it on the line. <bookmark mark='d'/> Clear, and resample again. Each resample is a dataset the population might plausibly have given us, if the population looked like the sample. Again. And again.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Do it two thousand times. The computer takes a fraction of a second. <bookmark mark='b'/> The bootstrap standard error is just the standard deviation of the two thousand resampled correlations: point one three five. <bookmark mark='c'/> The histogram is skewed to the left, because a correlation can't exceed one: the sampling distribution isn't normal, and the bootstrap shows it. <bookmark mark='d'/> The normal-theory formula said point one one five, <bookmark mark='e'/> the jackknife point one four three. Efron's paper used exactly this example, and found the same thing: a standard error for a statistic with no formula, or with a formula we don't trust, by brute force.

lines.raw: Efron's diagram makes the logic plain. <bookmark mark='a'/> In the real world, an unknown distribution F produces our sample, and the sample produces the estimate. If we could repeat that, we'd see the estimate's sampling distribution, but we get one sample. <bookmark mark='b'/> So build a stand-in for F from the sample: the empirical distribution, F-hat, which puts mass one over n on each observation. <bookmark mark='c'/> In the bootstrap world F-hat plays the part of the population. Sampling from it, with replacement, is resampling; and there we can repeat as often as we like. <bookmark mark='d'/> We want the distribution of the estimate's error under F, which we can't see. <bookmark mark='e'/> We can compute the distribution of the resampled estimate's error under F-hat. <bookmark mark='f'/> The bootstrap is the plug-in principle, Part 9's idea, applied to a whole sampling distribution: use the second as an estimate of the first. Part 30 will show when that's justified.

lines.raw: Can we check the principle? In the World, yes, because we can draw as many real samples as we like. <bookmark mark='a'/> The statistic is the median income, from samples of twenty-five. On the left, the real sampling distribution, two thousand samples from the World, centred on the true median of thirty-nine thousand. <bookmark mark='b'/> On the right, the bootstrap from a separate fixed sample, whose median is thirty-seven point seven. <bookmark mark='c'/> The real standard deviation is six point oh six; the bootstrap's, four point seven two. In the right ballpark, from one sample, but low. <bookmark mark='d'/> And the bootstrap histogram is spiky: the median of a resample can be any of the 25 sample values. These 2,000 replicates happen to visit sixteen of them. With a median and twenty-five observations, the bootstrap is rough. For smooth statistics like means and correlations it does much better.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> How many resamples? Fifteen schools can be drawn in fifteen to the fifteenth ordered ways; as unordered collections, there are seventy-seven million distinct resamples. <bookmark mark='b'/> The ideal bootstrap would average uniformly over ordered draws, or give unordered multisets their multinomial weights. They are not equally likely. <bookmark mark='c'/> Instead we sample B of them: Part 7's Monte Carlo, with error shrinking like one over root B. There are now two errors: the sampling error, from having one sample, which no amount of computing removes; and the Monte Carlo error, from finite B, which we can make as small as we like. <bookmark mark='d'/> For a regular distribution with finite fourth moments, a thousand resamples can give a standard error to within a few percent. Interval endpoints sit in the tails, where draws are scarce, and need a few thousand.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> What does the bootstrap assume? <bookmark mark='b'/> That the observations are independent draws from one distribution: you must resample in the way the data were sampled. Pairs stay pairs, as the law schools' LSAT and GPA did; clusters are resampled as clusters; time series need blocks, which is Part 17. <bookmark mark='c'/> That the empirical distribution is close to the real one, which needs a reasonable sample. <bookmark mark='d'/> And that the statistic depends smoothly on the distribution. Means and correlations do. A maximum doesn't, and chapter nine shows what happens then. <bookmark mark='e'/> What it doesn't assume is the gift: no normality, and no formula for the standard error.
lines.spoken: What does the bootstrap assume? That the observations are independent draws from one distribution: you must resample in the way the data were sampled. Pairs stay pairs, as the law schools' LSAT and GPA did; clusters are resampled as clusters; time series need blocks, which is Part 17. That the empirical distribution is close to the real one, which needs a reasonable sample. And that the statistic depends smoothly on the distribution. Means and correlations do. A maximum doesn't, and chapter nine shows what happens then. What it doesn't assume is the gift: no normality, and no formula for the standard error.
